title: Gendered language in performance feedback
text: Performance feedback shapes pay, promotion and development, yet research on gender bias in feedback mostly relies on small, manually coded samples. I set up a research collaboration with Culture Amp to study this question at scale, using natural language processing (NLP) on written feedback from organisations that use its platform. The work forms the core of my PhD at the University of Melbourne.

title: Gendered language in performance feedback
text:
The question
Do managers write about women and men differently, and does the manager’s own gender matter? I examine the content, tone and linguistic style of feedback, and the organisational factors, such as team size, that may explain gender differences.

title: Gendered language in performance feedback
text:
Approach

Text processing pipeline: cleaning, anonymisation and linguistic annotation of feedback texts (spaCy, LLM-based name extraction).
Content: agentic and communal language measured with sentence embeddings, distinctive vocabulary with weighted log-odds, and themes with topic modelling (NMF, BERTopic).
Tone: sentiment and emotion classified with transformer models (RoBERTa, GoEmotions), and valence and arousal scored with lexicons.
Style: hedging, elaboration, lexical diversity and grammatical complexity.
Inference: mixed-effects and GEE models that account for the clustering of feedback within manager–employee pairs, and mediation analysis for organisational mechanisms.

title: Gendered language in performance feedback
text:
Key findings

Manager gender often predicts feedback language more strongly than employee gender. Who writes the feedback matters as much as who receives it.
Female managers write longer, more positive feedback and hedge more, and hedging is strongest when female managers write about female employees.
Team size helps explain gender differences. Male managers oversee larger teams, and span of control partly accounts for differences in how managers frame their feedback.

title: Gendered language in performance feedback
text:
Why it matters
These findings suggest that efforts to reduce bias in performance reviews should look at the people who write feedback, not only at those who receive it. They also show how NLP can turn unstructured feedback into evidence that organisations can act on, for example in reviewer guidance, calibration sessions and DEI reporting.

title: Gendered language in performance feedback
text:
My role
I designed the research collaboration, built the full analysis pipeline in Python, and led all analyses and write-up, working with supervisors at the University of Melbourne and UC Berkeley Haas.

title: Noor de Bruijn
text: I am a data scientist and consultant based in Melbourne. I recently completed my PhD research at the University of Melbourne, where I applied natural language processing (NLP) to large-scale workplace text data. I also ran my own research and analytics firm for six years, working with clients in media, market research and e-commerce. My strengths: technical depth, practical problem-solving, and clear communication.
